statements: This community health advisory focuses on lung cancer prevention and early detection.
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death.
Most cases of lung cancer are linked to preventable risk factors.
Early detection through screening dramatically improves survival rates.
The biggest risk factors for lung cancer include smoking tobacco.
Smoking tobacco is the primary cause of lung cancer.
The risk of lung cancer rises with the number of cigarettes smoked and the number of years spent smoking.
Second-hand smoke exposure increases the risk of lung cancer for non-smokers.
Radon gas is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can accumulate in homes.

Occupational exposures to substances such as asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, silica, diesel fumes, and other fine particulate pollutants increase the risk of lung cancer.
Genetic predisposition, such as a family history of lung cancer or inherited mutations like BRCA2, raises the risk of lung cancer.
To reduce the risk of lung cancer, individuals should quit smoking.
Individuals seeking to quit smoking can seek counseling, nicotine-replacement therapy, or prescription medications.
Resources such as SmokeFree.gov and BeTobaccoFree.gov are available to assist individuals in quitting smoking.
Individuals should avoid second-hand smoke by staying in smoke-free environments.
Individuals should test for radon using a home radon test kit.
Individuals should remediate radon levels if they exceed the EPA action level of 4 pCi/L.
Individuals should use protective equipment, such as appropriate respirators, when working with known carcinogens.
Maintaining a healthy lifestyle, including regular exercise and a balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables, can lower overall cancer risk.
Screening recommendations for lung cancer include low-dose computed tomography (LDCT).

Individuals aged 50 to 80 years should undergo annual low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) of the chest if they have a 20 pack-year smoking history and are current smokers or have quit within the past 15 years.
Younger adults with high-risk occupational exposure or a strong family history of lung cancer should discuss individualized screening with their health-care provider.
Routine LDCT is not recommended for individuals with no smoking history, who should focus on risk-reduction measures.
After a screening, individuals with a negative result should repeat LDCT annually while eligibility criteria are met.
Individuals with a positive or indeterminate finding will have follow-up imaging, possible biopsy, or referral to a lung-cancer specialist arranged by their provider.
Early warning signs of lung cancer include a persistent cough that does not improve.
Coughing up blood, also known as hemoptysis, is an early warning sign of lung cancer.
Unexplained weight loss can be an early warning sign of lung cancer.
New or worsening shortness of breath is an early warning sign of lung cancer.
Constant chest pain or chest pain that worsens with breathing can indicate lung cancer.
Hoarseness or changes in voice can be an early warning sign of lung cancer.
Recurrent pneumonia or bronchitis can be an early warning sign of lung cancer.
Individuals experiencing any of these symptoms should contact their health-care provider promptly for evaluation.
Individuals should assess their risk by considering their smoking history, home radon levels, occupational exposures, and family history.
Individuals should schedule screening if they meet the LDCT criteria.

statements: Lung cancer forms in the cells lining the airways of the lungs.
Early detection of lung cancer before symptoms develop offers the best chance for successful treatment and mortality reduction.
Smoking tobacco is the single largest risk factor for lung cancer.
Tobacco smoke contains more than 50 known cancer-causing compounds.
The risk of lung cancer increases the more and the longer a person smokes.
Exposure to secondhand smoke from the burning end of tobacco products or exhaled smoke raises the risk of lung cancer.
Prevention of lung cancer starts by never starting smoking.
Quitting smoking lowers the likelihood of developing new lung tumors.
Medical providers can offer counseling and medications to help individuals quit smoking.
The risk of lung cancer also increases with exposure to environmental and workplace cancer-causing agents.

Environmental and workplace cancer-causing agents include radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and air pollution consisting of fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide.
Other contributing risk factors for lung cancer include being over 70 years of age, prior radiation therapy to the chest, and inherited genetic traits.
Lung cancer screening is not recommended for everyone.
Lung cancer screening is specifically for individuals identified as high risk based on their risk factors.
The goal of lung cancer screening is to identify cancer at an early, highly treatable stage before any symptoms appear.
Community members should see their healthcare providers regularly.
Community members should keep their healthcare providers updated on family health history.
Community members should consult their healthcare providers to determine individual risk levels and eligibility for lung cancer screening.
Lung cancer, including rapidly growing small cell lung cancer, is often only diagnosed after symptoms arise or routine blood tests become abnormal.
Symptoms of lung cancer depend on where the tumor has grown or spread.
Tumors can prevent the lungs from getting the air they need.
Abnormal body responses to lung cancer can produce paraneoplastic syndromes.
Community members experiencing breathing difficulties or other concerning symptoms should immediately consult their healthcare provider for evaluation.
